one_liner: CloudWeGo's Rust Thrift/gRPC framework. Self-reports 350k QPS on a 4-core 1KB Thrift echo, about 1.5x Kitex's published pingpong number.
what_it_does: Volo is a Rust RPC framework for microservices. It is made of volo-thrift (Thrift), volo-grpc (gRPC on hyper 1.x/h2) and volo-http, plus volo-build and volo-cli, which use Pilota to generate typed clients and service traits from Thrift or protobuf IDL. You implement the generated async service trait, build clients with a generated ClientBuilder, and write middleware as Motore Service/Layer types (AFIT/RPITIT, no boxing). It is not a drop-in for Kitex (Go), but it speaks the same wire formats, including Kitex's TTHeader, so Volo and Kitex services can call each other.
how_it_is_fast: The Thrift path uses a zero-copy codec. The encoder first computes the exact message size and reserves one buffer. It then splices large Bytes/FastStr fields into a LinkedBytes chain (the recommended threshold is 4KB) and flushes it with vectored writes (writev), while the decoder hands out Bytes::split_to slices of the read buffer instead of copying. An opt-in unsafe-codec feature switches to Pilota's unchecked binary protocol, and the in-repo benchmark turns it on. Static dispatch through AFIT/RPITIT middleware, per-connection Tokio tasks with pooled client connections, and a release profile with lto=true and codegen-units=1 keep framework overhead low; the README says it is 'basically negligible (excluding syscall overhead)' in production flame graphs.
when_to_use: Writing Thrift RPC services in Rust, especially ones that must call or be called by Kitex (Go) services over TTHeader or Framed Binary.
Moving a CPU-bound Kitex Thrift service with small (~1KB) request/response bodies to Rust to raise per-core QPS.
Services whose governance (timeouts, load balancing including consistent hash, discovery) is written as statically dispatched middleware layers.
Same-host RPC, where Unix domain sockets or the optional shmipc shared-memory transport (built only on Linux in CI) avoid the TCP loopback path.
when_not_to_use: When you need a published head-to-head benchmark. The README gives only Volo's own QPS, with no CPU, rustc version, concurrency or connection mode and no Kitex number, and the repo has no committed Volo results.
gRPC-only services chosen for speed: volo-grpc is built on hyper/h2 and has no benchmark of its own.
When you need registries out of the box: the ROADMAP still lists etcd, ZooKeeper, Nacos, Polaris, Eureka and Consul discovery as not done (issues #71, #475).
32-bit targets: volo-thrift pulls in sonic-rs, whose sonic-simd dependency fails on i686, and the maintainers have no plan for 32-bit (issue #543).

Very high fan-out clients that need a hard connection cap. The Thrift pool Config only has max_idle_per_key (default 10240) and an idle timeout, with no limit on total connections, and one user reported tens of thousands of TIME_WAIT sockets (open issue #641).

integration.dependencies: tokio, motore, pilota (IDL codegen and codec), metainfo, faststr, linkedbytes, socket2, nix, libc. volo-thrift adds sonic-rs; volo-grpc adds hyper 1.x, h2 and tower (tonic/tonic-web only for the optional grpc-web feature). TLS is optional via rustls (aws-lc-rs or ring) or native-tls, and shmipc is optional.
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.85.0 stable (workspace rust-version, edition 2024); CI tests on stable and nightly
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 is fully tested in CI. Linux aarch64, macOS and Windows are build/clippy-checked only (--no-test), and macOS and Windows are checked without shmipc. 32-bit x86 does not build (issue #543).
integration.thread_safety: Clients are Clone and shared across tasks (the benchmark clones one client across workers). #[volo::main] is a re-export of tokio::main, and the server spawns one Tokio task per accepted connection.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — wire-compatible with Kitex (Thrift Binary/Compact over Framed or TTHeader), so the two can call each other, but services must be rewritten in Rust from the same IDL

gotchas: The default codec is TTHeader<Framed<Binary>>, and TTHeader is a CloudWeGo-private header that only Volo and Kitex understand. Clients calling plain Apache Thrift servers need DefaultMakeCodec::framed() or ::buffered(). Servers auto-detect TTHeader, Framed, and Binary/Compact/FBThrift-compact, and the default max frame size is 16MB.

unsafe-codec (the benchmark build uses it) 'may cause undefined behavior if the thrift message is malformed'. unsafe_unchecked swaps unreachable!() for unreachable_unchecked. Keep both off on endpoints that receive untrusted input.

Multiplexing is behind the 'multiplex' feature, off by default, and documented as unstable with no backward-compatibility promise. The in-repo benchmark compiles it in but runs a pingpong pooled client with the Framed codec.
The 440k QPS figure is a Monoio-based internal build. The published crates are Tokio-only (monoio is not a workspace dependency), so expect the 350k-class number at most.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Volo over Kitex when you want Rust and about 1.5x Kitex's pingpong QPS (Volo's 350k vs Kitex's published ~229k) while you stay wire-compatible with a Kitex/TTHeader fleet; Kitex-MUX's 396-410k is still higher. Pick it over SRPC or brpc when the stack is Rust rather than C++. For gRPC-only Rust servers, wtx has a direct grpc-go comparison and Volo does not.
verified_claims_summary: Volo's README self-reports 350k QPS for a 1KB Thrift echo with the server limited to 4 cores 'under the same test conditions as Kitex' (440k for an unreleased Monoio build), but names no CPU, rustc version, concurrency or connection mode. Kitex's matching 2022 report (Xeon Gold 5118, server 4 CPUs, Go 1.17.2) shows about 228-231k pingpong QPS, which makes Volo about 1.5x (derived from page data), while Kitex-MUX reaches 396-410k at 400-1000 concurrency.
status_note: Actively maintained (last main commit 2026-08-31, volo-thrift 0.12.6 on crates.io with about 485k total downloads) and dual-licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0, but every crate is pre-1.0 and the performance text dates from 2022 and has not been re-run.
